problem_data.story:
QUANTUM COLLAPSE
BY ELENA HAYES

The server banks hummed in their climate-controlled chambers, processing petabytes of data every microsecond. In the Summit District headquarters of Nexus Corporation, the most advanced quantum computing facility ever built sat silent and dark, its supercooled processors offline for the first time in three years.

Dr. Hassan McCoy pressed his hand against the observation window, staring at the dormant machine that had been his life's work. Behind him, the emergency recorder continued its documentation.

"This is Dr. Hassan McCoy, lead physicist on Project Quantum Bridge, recording for the incident investigation. I reached this emergency shelter sometime after midnight, though I can't be certain of the exact hour. The facility's atomic clock read 23:47 when the explosion hit yesterday—March 14th, 2157. That timestamp will be burned into my memory forever.

"I'm probably the only survivor, and I need to get this on record while I still can. I've been awake for over thirty hours now. The sun rose about two hours ago, and I watched it through the shelter's viewport while I gathered my thoughts. I couldn't sleep—every time I closed my eyes, I saw Dr. Rodriguez's face in those final moments.

"You're probably wondering what went wrong. How did the most secure facility in Nordavia, with triple-redundant systems and the best cybersecurity protocols ever designed, end up completely compromised? How did six people die and the entire quantum network collapse?

"I'll tell you how. We got cocky. We thought we understood particle physics well enough to build a bridge between quantum states. We thought our laboratory methods were foolproof. We were wrong on both counts.

"Let me start at the beginning. Project Quantum Bridge was designed to create stable quantum entanglement across macroscopic distances. Not just photons or electrons, but actual information systems. Imagine instant communication across any distance, unhackable encryption, processing power that makes our current systems look like abacuses. That's what we promised, and that's what we delivered. For three years, it worked perfectly.

"The breakthrough came from applying systems thinking to quantum mechanics. Instead of treating particles as isolated units, we modeled the entire quantum field as an interconnected system. Dr. Jin Brooks led that work—brilliant woman, background in both particle physics and cultural anthropology of all things. She argued that quantum systems behaved like social networks, with information propagating through relationship structures rather than linear pathways. Sounds crazy, but it worked.

"We built the Bridge in stages. First facility here in Summit District, second in Morningside, Nordavia, third in Yarnmouth, Quendor, and the final node in Crystalbrook District. Four quantum processors, entangled at the substrate level, sharing computational states instantaneously across thousands of miles.

"The applications were revolutionary. Consumer behavior prediction became trivially easy when you could process every transaction in real-time across the entire network. Economic development models that used to take months to run completed in seconds. We were going to change the world.

"Then the Yarnmouth facility reported anomalies. Dr. Talia Bailey was running the night shift when she noticed strange patterns in the quantum foam—fluctuations that shouldn't exist in a properly isolated system. She ran diagnostics for six hours before calling it in. Everything checked out normal, but the fluctuations persisted.

"We should have shut down then. We didn't.

"Two weeks later, Dr. Laura Rodriguez in Morningside reported similar issues. Then Crystalbrook. Then us. The fluctuations were spreading, synchronizing across all four nodes. Dr. Brooks proposed that we were seeing quantum decoherence from an external source, but we couldn't identify what. Our cybersecurity team, led by Stephen Nelson, ran every penetration test in the book. Nothing. The systems were secure.

"That's when Yuki Wallace arrived.

"Yuki came from the Yarnmouth facility as a 'consultant.' That's what they called her, anyway. She had credentials in material science and design thinking, supposedly there to help us optimize our cooling systems. But she spent most of her time just watching us work, asking odd questions, laughing at private jokes.

"I didn't trust her from the start. There was something off about her timing, her questions, the way she always seemed to be around when things went wrong. When Dr. Rodriguez's terminal crashed during a critical calculation, Yuki was standing right behind her. When the Crystalbrook link went unstable, Yuki had been 'consulting' there the day before. When our primary cooling system developed a leak, Yuki had just finished 'inspecting' it.

"But every incident checked out as equipment failure or human error. Rodriguez admitted she'd been working eighteen-hour shifts and might have made a mistake. The Crystalbrook instability traced back to a miscalibrated sensor. The cooling leak was a faulty seal, batch defect from the manufacturer.

"Plausible. All of it plausible.

"I started keeping notes. Yuki never made mistakes herself, but people around her did. Equipment near her failed. Calculations went wrong. It was subtle, distributed, deniable. But it was consistent.

"I researched her background. Her credentials were legitimate, but sparse. She'd worked on three major projects before ours. All three had experienced catastrophic failures attributed to improbable chains of human error and equipment malfunction.

"I tried to tell Dr. Brooks. She laughed it off. 'You're seeing patterns that aren't there, Hassan. That's not science, that's paranoia.' She was right, of course. I had no evidence, just statistical inference from anecdotal data. Not enough to accuse someone of... what? Being unlucky?

"The final test was scheduled for yesterday—Tuesday, March 14th. We were going to demonstrate full quantum coherence across all four nodes simultaneously—a complete merging of computational states. The processing power would be unprecedented. We'd already lined up demonstrations for the Nordavian government, the Economic Development Council, even representatives from the Justice Theory Institute who wanted to model legal frameworks.

"Yuki was very interested in the test. She asked detailed questions about the timing, the protocols, the safety margins. She wanted to know what would happen if coherence failed during the merge. We told her: catastrophic decoherence, possible damage to the quantum processors, but the containment systems would prevent any danger to personnel.

"We were wrong about that too.

"The test began at 14:00 hours on the 14th. All four facilities confirmed ready status. Dr. Brooks initiated the coherence sequence from the Summit District control room. I was monitoring the quantum field topology from my station. Stephen Nelson watched the security systems. Laura Rodriguez and Talia Bailey were on video link from their facilities. Yuki stood in the back of the control room, observing.

"For thirty seconds, it was beautiful. Perfect coherence across all nodes. The quantum field stabilized into a unified structure spanning thousands of miles. Processing power spiked to theoretical maximum. We were cheering.

"Then the fluctuations returned. Not gradually this time—all at once, everywhere. The quantum foam began to boil. Decoherence spread through the system like a virus. Dr. Brooks tried to abort, but the safety protocols failed. The containment fields failed. The backup systems failed.

"Everything failed at once.

"The quantum processors began to cascade. When quantum states collapse chaotically, they release energy. A lot of energy. The Yarnmouth facility exploded first. Dr. Bailey's video feed went white, then black. Crystalbrook went next. Then Morningside—I watched Dr. Rodriguez's face as she realized what was happening, watched her try to run, watched the feed cut out.

"Our facility was last. Dr. Brooks was screaming at her terminal, trying to engage manual overrides that wouldn't respond. Stephen Nelson was pulling people toward the exits. The quantum core was glowing, temperature spiking past every safety threshold.

"I looked back and saw Yuki. She was smiling. Not laughing, not gloating—just smiling, like she'd solved a particularly interesting puzzle. Then she turned and walked calmly toward the emergency stairs.

"I ran. We all ran. The explosion caught us in the stairwell. The blast wave threw me down three flights. When I woke up, I was buried in rubble, my left arm broken, my hazmat suit torn but functional. I could hear small fires crackling, structural elements groaning. No voices.

"I dug myself out. Took four hours—didn't emerge until well after dark. The facility was destroyed. I found Dr. Brooks near the control room—she hadn't made it far. Stephen Nelson was in the stairwell below me. I couldn't find the others, and I couldn't stay to look. The structure was collapsing.

"I made it to the surface access tunnel and sealed it behind me. I reached this emergency shelter around 0200 hours—middle of the night, the 14th bleeding into the 15th. I've got power, water, medical supplies. I've been trying to reach someone, anyone, on the emergency channels. Nothing but static.

"I've spent the hours since arriving thinking about Yuki Wallace. About her pattern of failures. About how quantum mechanics describes probability, and how probability is just another word for chance, and how chance is just another word for luck.

"What if luck isn't random? What if it's a field effect, like gravity or electromagnetism? What if some people can manipulate probability the way we manipulate quantum states?

"It sounds insane. But consider: quantum mechanics tells us that reality is probabilistic at the fundamental level. Every particle exists in a superposition of states until observation collapses the wave function. What determines which state manifests? Probability. Pure chance.

"But what if it's not pure? What if consciousness can bias quantum outcomes, nudge probability in preferred directions? We've known about observer effects in quantum mechanics for two centuries. We've documented quantum consciousness theories, though most are dismissed as pseudoscience. But what if, on some world we haven't discovered yet, in some population we haven't encountered, this talent evolved? Developed? Became reliable?

"Yuki Wallace destroyed four quantum facilities and killed six people without touching anything, without hacking anything, without breaking any laws. She just walked through our facility and let probability do the work. Equipment failed. People made mistakes. Safety systems didn't trigger. All improbable, but not impossible. Just... unlucky.

"I can't prove it. I have no evidence that would stand up to scientific scrutiny. But I know what I saw, and I know the pattern. Check her background. Check the other facilities she's worked at. Look for the improbable chains of failure.

"And if you find her, if you track her down, remember this: a talent that manipulates probability can't be perfect. It's bound by the same quantum uncertainty it exploits. She can bias outcomes, but she can't control them absolutely. The proof is that I survived to tell this story.

"I'm going to try to reach Morningside on foot. It's forty miles through rough terrain, but I've got supplies and the suit's environmental systems are still functional. If I don't make it, if this recording is all that's left, then at least someone will know what happened.

"This is Dr. Hassan McCoy. Recording timestamp shows 0847 hours—morning of the day after everything ended. God help us if there are more like her."

The recording clicked off. In the emergency shelter, Hassan McCoy checked his supplies one more time, adjusted his damaged hazmat suit, and prepared to begin the long walk to Morningside. Outside, the wind howled across the wasteland that had been Summit District's pride, carrying radioactive dust from the shattered quantum facility.

He didn't know that Yuki Wallace was already in Morningside, consulting on their new fusion project. He didn't know that the probability of his survival, given his injuries and the distance, was less than three percent. He didn't know that his emergency beacon, which he believed was malfunctioning, was actually working perfectly—but every rescue team that tried to respond encountered improbable equipment failures and navigational errors.

Hassan McCoy shouldered his pack and started walking. He was a scientist. He believed in evidence, in causation, in the rational universe. He believed that luck was just a word people used for patterns they didn't understand yet.

He believed he would make it to Morningside.

He was wrong.

But he was right about Yuki Wallace, and his recording would eventually reach people who could act on it. In the end, that would have to be enough.

Three miles into his journey, Hassan McCoy activated his suit recorder one final time:

"Additional note for the record. I've been thinking about political philosophy, about how we organize society around the assumption that everyone plays by the same rules of physics. What happens when someone doesn't? When someone can manipulate the fundamental probability structure of reality?

"Justice theory assumes equality before natural law. Economic development assumes predictable cause and effect. Communication skills mean nothing if someone can make your words come out wrong. Environmental justice is impossible if disasters can be caused by pure bad luck.

"We built our entire civilization on the assumption that chance is truly random. If it's not, if it can be controlled, then everything changes. Every system, every institution, every assumption about how the world works needs to be reconsidered.

"I don't have answers. I just have questions and a warning: Yuki Wallace is out there, and she's not alone. There must be others. And until we figure out how to detect them, how to defend against them, we're all vulnerable.

"The most dangerous weapon is the one you don't know exists.

"Dr. Hassan McCoy, final entry. The calendar on my suit display has flipped to the 15th now—feels like a lifetime since yesterday's test, though it's barely been eighteen hours since everything went wrong."

The wind picked up, carrying snow across the desolate landscape. Hassan McCoy continued walking, his footprints quickly filling with white powder. Behind him, the ruins of the quantum facility smoldered. Ahead, Morningside waited—forty miles away, impossible to reach, but he would try anyway.

Because he was a scientist, and scientists don't give up just because the odds are bad.

Even when the odds aren't random at all.
